Courtly describes a style of behavior that is very polished, refined, and elegantly formal — the kind of gracious, almost ceremonious politeness associated with royal courts and aristocratic life. When you call someone or something courtly, you are saying that there is a certain dignified, old-world charm to the way they carry themselves or speak.

Think of it this way: "polite" is a broad word covering everything from holding a door open to saying "please." Courtly is something much more specific — it is politeness raised to an art form, practiced with deliberate grace and careful attention to manner. It suggests smooth, careful gestures, measured and elegant words, and a kind of attentive respectfulness that feels almost ceremonial.
What It Looks Like in Practice

A courtly person might:

  • Bow slightly when greeting someone, rather than just nodding
  • Speak with great care and choose flattering, formal words
  • Pull out a chair, offer a hand, hold open a door — but do all of this with a certain deliberate elegance, not casually
  • Compliment others in elaborate, gracious terms
  • Conduct themselves as though every interaction deserves a certain ceremony and dignity

You would not describe a teenager being courtly to their friend in a text message. You would describe an elderly diplomat who greets every guest with the same unhurried, careful warmth. Or a character in a historical novel who bows and speaks with formality at every turn.
The Full Range of Its Meaning

Courtly can carry two slightly different shades depending on context:

Positively: It describes someone who is impressively refined, dignified, and gracious — a person with beautiful manners and an effortless elegance that commands respect. This is the most common use. A "courtly gentleman" or "courtly manner" is a genuine compliment here.

With a mild edge of irony or skepticism: Sometimes "courtly" hints at manners that are too polished — overly smooth, flattering, or even a little calculated. The person is being almost performatively gracious, putting on a show of elegance. In this sense, courtly politeness can feel slightly hollow or sycophantic — charming on the surface but perhaps not entirely genuine underneath. This shade of meaning doesn't always appear, but it is there in certain contexts, so pay attention to tone.
"Courtly Love" — A Fixed Phrase Worth Knowing

One important and very common use of courtly is in the phrase courtly love. This refers to a specific tradition from medieval European literature and culture — a highly idealized, formal style of romantic devotion. In courtly love, a knight (or nobleman) would dedicate himself completely to a noblewoman, worship her from a respectful distance, write poetry in her honor, and perform noble deeds to prove his devotion — all within a strict set of social rituals. The love was often unrequited, spiritual, and elevated rather than physical. This tradition shaped centuries of poetry, chivalry, and ideas about romance.

When people use "courtly love" today, they usually refer to this medieval tradition specifically, or they use it to describe any romantic relationship that is notably formal, elevated, idealized, and conducted with great ceremony and restraint.

• He greeted every guest with a courtly bow and a warm, measured smile.
  • Her writing had a courtly elegance — every sentence felt deliberate and refined.
  • The old professor had a courtly way about him: always careful with his words, always attentive.
  • His courtly charm was impressive, though some found it a little too smooth to be entirely real.
  • The poem was written in the tradition of courtly love, full of devotion and longing from afar.
The Big Picture — When and Why This Word Is Used

You will mostly encounter courtly in:

  • Literature and history — describing characters, aristocrats, nobles, or knights and their behavior
  • Descriptions of people — especially older people or those who carry an old-fashioned, formal dignity
  • Cultural or literary analysis — particularly "courtly love" as a medieval concept
  • Everyday admiration — to compliment someone whose manners feel unusually graceful and refined

The word always carries that sense of a certain era — it brings to mind royal halls, careful formality, and a time when elegance of manner was considered a high virtue. When used today, it often suggests that someone is a bit of a throwback: admirably, charmingly out of step with the casual modern world.

In one sentence: Courtly means polished, graciously formal, and elegantly refined in manners or behavior — like someone who has turned politeness into an art, with the dignity and ceremony of a royal court.
